content: Endometriosis is a medical condition in which functional endometrial tissue, which normally lines the inside of the uterus, is found outside the uterine cavity. The most commonly affected areas include the ovaries, broad ligaments, and other pelvic structures. In some cases, endometriosis can also involve distant sites such as the lungs, ureters, or even the central nervous system. The exact mechanism by which endometriosis develops is not fully understood, but several theories have been proposed. These include the Sampson theory of retrograde menstruation, the coelomic metaplasia theory, and the lymphatic and vascular dissemination theory, all of which attempt to explain how endometrial tissue implants and invades areas outside the uterus. Endometriosis is a significant cause of dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation) and dyspareunia (pain during intercourse). It is important to distinguish endometriosis from other conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as adenomyosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, pelvic congestion syndrome, and submucosal uterine fibroids. The primary goals of treatment are to manage pain and reduce the size of the endometrial implants. Medical therapies include the use of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists and danazol. Surgical intervention is typically reserved for patients with severe disease or those who do not respond to medical treatment. Historically, endometriosis was first described in the early 19th century as adenomyomas. By the 1920s, it was differentiated from adenomyosis, and detailed descriptions of the disease were provided by Cullen and Sampson. Sampson also introduced the retrograde menstruation theory as a potential explanation for the disease's pathogenesis. Endometriosis is classified into four stages of severity based on the revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) scoring system. This classification is determined by the distribution of lesions and the presence of adhesions. The pathophysiology of endometriosis remains unclear, but several theories have been proposed to explain its development. These include retrograde menstruation, coelomic metaplasia, and lymphatic or vascular dissemination. Additionally, immunologic and genetic factors are believed to contribute to the disease's pathogenesis. The exact cause of endometriosis is unknown, but it is thought to have a multifactorial origin. Endometriosis affects approximately 11% of women of reproductive age. It is more commonly observed in Caucasian women compared to African American women. The condition is a leading cause of chronic pelvic pain and infertility. Risk factors for developing endometriosis include early onset of menstruation, nulliparity (never having given birth), a family history of the condition, and congenital abnormalities such as cervical stenosis or obstructive lesions in the uterovaginal tract. Routine screening for endometriosis is not recommended. The clinical presentation of endometriosis varies widely. Some women may be asymptomatic, while others experience symptoms such as premenstrual spotting, cyclic abdominal pain, infertility, or chronic pelvic pain. Severe cases may present with deep endometriosis, characterized by dyspareunia, dyschezia (painful bowel movements), and cyclic rectal bleeding. Complications of endometriosis include infertility, the formation of fibrotic tissue, the development of chocolate cysts (endometriomas), and, in rare cases, involvement of other organs such as the lungs. The diagnosis of endometriosis begins with a thorough history and physical examination. Patients may report a family history of the condition or congenital abnormalities such as cervical stenosis. Common symptoms include cyclical abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, pain during bowel movements, and pain during intercourse. On physical examination, findings may include a fixed retroverted uterus, palpable nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments, and narrowing of the posterior fornix. Laboratory findings in endometriosis may reveal iron deficiency anemia and elevated levels of cancer antigen-125 (CA-125) and interleukin-1. There are no specific electrocardiogram (EKG) findings associated with endometriosis. On chest X-ray, endometriosis involving the lungs may present as small bubbles near the right diaphragm, often associated with pneumothorax. Computed tomography (CT) is not the most sensitive imaging modality for diagnosing endometriosis, but it may reveal findings such as catamenial pneumothorax, hemothorax, or lung nodules. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more useful for assessing the anatomical location and severity of the disease. Endometriosis typically appears as hyperintense lesions on T1-weighted images and hypointense lesions on T2-weighted images. Ultrasound, particularly transvaginal ultrasound, is helpful in differentiating endometriosis from other cystic lesions of the female reproductive system. Endometrial lesions often show increased vascularity and Doppler flow. The gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis is diagnostic laparoscopy, which allows direct visualization of the extent and severity of the disease. The primary goal of medical therapy for endometriosis is to manage pain and reduce the size of endometrial lesions. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are commonly used for pain relief. Other therapeutic options include GnRH agonists, danazol, and continuous use of oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for patients with mild to moderate disease. Surgical therapy is indicated for patients who do not respond to medical treatment or those with advanced-stage disease (stage 3 or 4). Surgical options include laser ablation or excision of isolated lesions, while total hysterectomy may be necessary for patients with extensive disease.
